readerTitle: Why eBay lost China to a free website
caseNote: 실제 기업 (eBay와 Taobao, Uber와 Didi) + 실제 연구 (Dawar & Frost 1999) + 가상 적용 (급여 대행사, 동네 수리업체)
insight: 새 시장에서 싸울 진짜 상대는 다른 글로벌 기업이 아니라, 그 시장에 딱 맞춰 자란 현지 강자다. 기준은 내 규모가 아니라 그들이 맞춘 정도다.
misconception: 자금, 브랜드, 기술이 더 큰 글로벌 기업이 들어가면 작은 현지 기업은 결국 밀려난다.

sources.text: Dawar, N. & Frost, T. (1999). Competing with Giants: Survival Strategies for Local Companies in Emerging Markets. Harvard Business Review.
eBay 연례 보고서 및 보도자료 (EachNet 인수 2003년, Tom Online 합작 2006년)
Uber와 Didi Chuxing 보도자료 (2016년 8월, Uber China 매각)

factChecks.note: eBay는 2002년 EachNet 지분 일부를 사고 2003년 나머지를 인수했습니다. 2006년 12월 Tom Online과 합작사를 세우며 중국 사이트 운영을 넘겼습니다. 날짜와 표현을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
Taobao는 2003년 Alibaba가 시작했고 판매자 등록 수수료가 무료였습니다. 채팅 도구(Wangwang)와 대금 보관 결제(Alipay)는 널리 보도된 내용이지만 도입 시점은 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에서는 시점을 적지 않았습니다.
eBay가 EachNet을 글로벌 플랫폼으로 옮긴 일(2004년경)과 그로 인한 사용성 문제는 여러 사례 연구에 나오지만 영향의 크기는 확인하기 어렵습니다. 카드에는 일반적으로만 적었습니다. 시장 점유율 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
Uber는 2016년 중국 사업을 Didi에 넘기고 Didi 지분을 받았습니다. 지분율 등 세부 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
Dawar & Frost 연구의 요지(현지 자산이 중요한 영역에서 현지 기업이 버틸 수 있다)를 일반적으로만 소개했습니다. 원문의 네 가지 전략 이름은 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why eBay lost China to a free website
body: In 2003, eBay bought China's leading online auction site. It had the money, the brand and the know-how of the world's biggest online marketplace.
A few years later, it handed its China site to a local partner. The winner was a newcomer that started the same year eBay bought in.

image.label: A giant ship stuck while a small boat moves through a narrow river
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 좁고 구불구불한 강에서 거대한 화물선이 모래톱에 걸려 있고, 작은 현지 배가 물길을 따라 쉽게 지나가는 장면. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A small local firm stands in your way.
body: You run a payroll and HR services firm in eight countries. You enter a ninth. One local firm dominates. It's a tenth your size, but local accountants recommend it, and it handles the country's odd filing rules.
How do you plan to win?

options.text: Undercut its prices for two years with your bigger budget
options.feedback: You may buy some customers, but you don't fix why they chose the local firm. When prices rise again, many may return.

options.text: Lead with your global platform and brand
options.feedback: That helps with clients who work across borders. Most local clients care more about filings done right and an accountant they trust.

options.text: Find out exactly why clients pick the local firm, then match or beat those reasons first
options.feedback: Slower and less exciting, but it aims at the rival's real strength. It may even show that partnering or buying is smarter than fighting.

cards.title: The local rival fit the market better.
body: Alibaba launched Taobao in 2003. Sellers could list for free. Buyers and sellers could chat directly, which Chinese shoppers liked for bargaining. A payment service held the money until the goods arrived, which built trust between strangers.

eBay charged fees and moved its China site onto its global platform, designed for other markets. By the end of 2006, eBay had passed its China site to a joint venture with a local company. Taobao went on to become one of the largest online marketplaces in the world.

cards.title: Local champions
body: A **local champion** is a home-grown firm whose strength comes from fitting its own market closely: local habits, relationships, rules and fast decisions made close to customers.
A global entrant brings scale. The local champion brings fit. When customers care most about fit, scale doesn't win on its own.

image.label: Two columns: global strengths vs local strengths
image.brief: 두 칸 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Global entrant": 큰 자금, 브랜드, 표준 플랫폼. 오른쪽 "Local champion": 현지 습관, 관계, 규칙 이해, 빠른 결정. 가운데 저울이 "What customers value most" 쪽으로 기울어짐.

cards.title: It isn't one unlucky company.
body: In 2016, Uber sold its China business to local rival Didi Chuxing, taking a stake in Didi instead of fighting on.

In a 1999 Harvard Business Review article, Niraj Dawar and Tony Frost studied local firms in emerging markets facing multinationals. Their point: local firms can hold their ground where local knowledge and relationships matter most, instead of competing head-on on scale.

cards.title: Every market has a local champion.
body: You don't need to cross a border to meet one. A national chain opening in a new town faces the bakery everyone grew up with, or the accountant who knows every shop owner by name.
The question is the same either way: what does the local favorite understand that you don't yet?
cards.softwareNote: Global apps often meet local rivals built around local payment methods, languages and messaging habits. Before launch, list the features local users expect that your product doesn't have.

cards.title: Local isn't a permanent shield.
body: Global firms often win where the product is the same everywhere and scale lowers costs. Think of phones, cars or cloud storage.
And local champions can grow lazy. If their only advantage is being there first, a patient entrant that learns the market can overtake them.
So don't conclude that locals always win. Ask where the advantage really comes from, and whether it can be copied.

cards.title: Now you're the local champion.
body: You own a well-loved home repair business in an old city. A national chain arrives with a booking app, big ads and lower prices.

options.text: Cut prices to match the chain
options.feedback: You fight where the chain is strongest. Its scale lets it outlast you on price, and you lose margin you need to keep good staff.

options.text: Build your own app and match its ad spending
options.feedback: Easy booking matters, and a simple online form is worth adding. But a spending race plays to the chain's size, not your strengths.

options.text: Lean into what you know: old houses, same-day visits, referrals from local agents, plus simple online booking
options.feedback: You defend the ground where local knowledge counts. You fix the one gap that matters without copying the chain's whole model.

cards.title: Size the local champion's fit, not your own size.
body: In a new market, the strongest rival is often the one who knows it best. Learn why customers choose them before you plan how to win.
**Try it today:** name the local favorite in a market you want to enter or defend. Write three reasons customers pick it. Which can you match, and which can't you?
